sms.title: Scam Text Messages UK: Spot, Check & Report
sms.description: A scam text? Learn the UK smishing patterns — fake delivery, bank, HMRC and DVLA texts — how to check a suspicious message safely, and how to report it to 7726.
sms.intro:
Scam texts — known as smishing (SMS phishing) — are widely encountered in the UK. In a survey conducted for Ofcom in February 2026, 40% of UK mobile users said they had received at least one suspicious message in the previous three months. A message pretends to be a courier, your bank, HMRC, the DVLA or the NHS, and pushes you to tap a link, pay a small fee, or hand over a code. The golden rule never changes: never act on the link, phone number or payment details inside the message itself — open the official app or website yourself and check. This hub explains the texts doing the rounds in the UK, how to tell a fake from the real thing, and how to report one in under a minute.

Not sure about a message right now? Paste it into our free AI scam checker for an automated second opinion. It is not a verdict and does not replace checking through an official route yourself.
sections: The most common UK scam texts

Fake delivery texts are a very common category — a 'missed parcel', 'redelivery fee' or 'address problem' from a courier you may not even be expecting. See the guides for DPD, Evri (formerly Hermes), Yodel, UPS and Royal Mail.

Bank texts claim there's 'suspicious activity' or a 'new payee', or ask you to 'verify' your account — and a related worry is when your genuine bank verification codes stop arriving. Bank-specific guides cover Halifax, Lloyds, NatWest and Barclays.

Government and council texts impersonate HMRC ('you're owed a tax refund'), the DVLA ('your vehicle tax failed'), the NHS and council tax departments — all leaning on a believable official name plus a link or a threat.
How to tell if a text is a scam

Scam texts often combine several warning signs. Treat a message as suspicious and verify it independently if any of these apply:

  • It contains a link asking you to pay, log in or 'verify'. Genuine organisations sometimes send links — HMRC lists genuine campaigns that may include GOV.UK information or webchat links — so the link alone is not proof; open the official app or website yourself instead.
  • It demands a small fee ('redelivery', 'release', 'customs') to free a parcel or fix an account.
  • It creates urgency — act within hours, your account will be closed, your parcel returned.
  • It comes from an ordinary mobile or international number when the organisation normally uses another channel. NCSC guidance says telecoms systems cannot reliably tell a recipient who originated a call or SMS, so a familiar sender name is not proof.
  • The web address isn't the official one — watch for extra words, hyphens or odd endings (e.g. 'royalmail-redelivery' rather than royalmail.com).
  • It asks for a full card number, PIN, password or one-time code. Never disclose these in response to an unexpected text.
How to check a suspicious text safely

Never tap the link. Verify the claim through a clean route you trust instead:

  • Go direct. Open the official app, or type the company's address into your browser yourself — never follow the link in the message.
  • Use the number you already have. Call the number on the back of your bank card, or the contact details on the official website — not a number from the text.
  • Check the order. For delivery texts, log into the retailer you actually bought from. No matching parcel is a strong warning rather than proof on its own — sender or courier information can be delayed or wrong — so check with the retailer and, if a delivery does exist, the courier's own official service.
  • Ask the checker. Paste the message into our free AI scam checker for an instant second opinion.
What to do if you've already tapped a link or paid

• If you entered card or bank details, contact your bank immediately on the number on your card — block the card and report fraud.
  • Change the password for any account whose details you entered, and turn on two-step verification.
  • Be ready for a follow-up phone call pretending to be your bank's fraud team — that's often stage two. Hang up and call your bank back on the official number.
  • Keep the message as evidence, then report it (below).
How to report a scam text in the UK

Reporting takes under a minute and genuinely helps providers investigate these campaigns.

  • Forward a suspicious SMS text to 7726 free of charge, as explained in Ofcom's current guidance. For RCS, iMessage and messages received through apps, use the service's built-in reporting tools.
  • Report to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or 0300 123 2040 if you've lost money or shared details (in Scotland, contact Police Scotland on 101).
  • Report phishing websites to the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC).
faq: Will my bank, Royal Mail or HMRC ever text me a link?

Genuine organisations may send texts and some include links. Do not decide from the presence of a link alone. Treat an unexpected link asking you to pay, log in or verify an account as suspicious; open the official app or website independently instead. Never disclose a full card number, PIN, password or one-time code in response to an unexpected text.
What is 7726 and how do I use it?

You can forward a suspicious SMS text to 7726 free of charge. The digits spell 'SPAM' on a phone keypad. RCS, iMessage and app messages use different systems, so report those with the relevant built-in reporting tool.
I clicked a link in a scam text — what should I do?

If you only opened the page, entered no information, downloaded, opened or installed nothing and granted no access, close it, report and delete the message, and remain alert for a follow-up. If you opened a file or attachment, installed software or a profile, granted a permission, allowed remote access, saw a security warning, or the device has since behaved oddly, treat it as a possible device compromise: disconnect it where appropriate, install pending updates, run the security checks your device or security software provides, remove anything you did not deliberately install, and change your passwords from a device you trust. If you allowed remote access, end the session first, remove or disable the remote-access software, secure your accounts from another trusted device, check your email forwarding and recovery settings, and get trusted technical help if access may persist. If you entered any card, bank or login details, contact your bank immediately on the number on your card, change the affected passwords, and turn on two-step verification. Watch for a follow-up call claiming to be your bank — that's part of the scam. Report it to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.
How do I know if a text is really from my bank?

A genuine bank text may use a named sender ID, but sender names and message threads can be spoofed, so neither is proof. Do not use an unexpected link to log in or verify an account. Open your banking app yourself or call the number on the back of your card to check.

payment.title: Payment Scams UK: Bank Transfer & APP Fraud
payment.description: Sent money to a scammer, or unsure about a payment request? Spot UK bank-transfer, APP, advance-fee and overpayment scams — how to check, stop and report them.
payment.intro:
Authorised push payment (APP) fraud is a major form of UK payment scam — the scammer doesn't hack your account, they trick you into authorising the payment or sending a bank transfer yourself, often by posing as your bank, a seller, a builder, or even the police. The golden rule: never move money because a call, text or email told you to — verify any payment request through a separate, trusted channel first.

Got a payment request you're unsure about? Paste it into our free AI scam checker for an automated second opinion. It is not a verdict and does not replace checking through an official route yourself.
sections: The most common UK payment scams

Bank-transfer scams include 'safe account' fraud, in which a caller claims money must be moved to protect it — our bank transfer and APP fraud guide explains the pattern and recovery options. Other frequent tricks include advance-fee scams, overpayment scams, invoice fraud, PayPal 'friends and family' scams, QR-code (quishing) scams and chargeback fraud.

Fake banking-app messages impersonate the apps people trust — Monzo, Revolut, Starling, Wise and Apple Pay — to push you into sending money or sharing codes.
How APP (authorised push payment) fraud works

In APP fraud the criminal convinces you to send the money yourself, so it looks authorised:

  • They impersonate someone you trust — your bank's fraud team, a tradesperson, a solicitor mid-house-purchase, a seller, or 'the police'.
  • They invent a reason to move money now: your account is 'compromised', an invoice's bank details have 'changed', or a fee is due.
  • The classic line is to move your money to a 'safe account' — there is no such thing, and your bank will never ask you to do this.
  • Because you pressed send, the payment is harder to reverse than a stolen-card transaction — which is exactly why scammers prefer it.
How to check a payment request safely

• Stop and verify independently. Hang up or close the message and contact the bank, company or person on a number or address you already have — never one supplied in the message.
  • Use Confirmation of Payee. If the account name doesn't match who you think you're paying, don't send.
  • Beware changed bank details. For invoices or deposits, confirm any 'new' account details by phone with a known contact before paying.
  • Call 159. Dialling 159 yourself connects you to a participating bank to check whether a call or request is genuine. Your phone provider sets the price of a 159 call and it may not be included in your allowance, so check its current charges.
  • Ask the checker. Run the message through our free AI scam checker first.
What to do if you've sent money to a scammer

• Contact your bank immediately — the sooner you report, the better the chance of stopping or tracing the payment. A claim normally must be made within 13 months of the last relevant payment.
  • Under the Payment Systems Regulator's protections, qualifying UK-to-UK Faster Payments and CHAPS APP claims made by individuals, microenterprises and charities have been covered since 7 October 2024. Reimbursement is normally expected within five business days of a claim, but a stop-clock of up to 35 business days, a possible excess of up to £100 (not for vulnerable consumers) and an £85,000 mandatory cap can apply. Card, cash and cheque payments, unauthorised fraud and ordinary civil disputes are outside this APP scheme. Complicity or gross negligence may prevent reimbursement; the PSR describes gross negligence as a high bar and says it does not apply to vulnerable consumers.
  • Report it to Report Fraud, or Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland, and keep all evidence — messages, payment details, account numbers.
  • Change passwords for any account whose details you shared and turn on two-step verification.
  • Watch for a follow-up 'we can recover your money' approach — recovery scams target people who've just been defrauded.
How to report payment fraud in the UK

Report to your bank first — they hold the reimbursement process and can try to stop the payment. If your bank supports it, call 159 to be connected safely to your bank, or use the number on your card. Your provider sets the price of a 159 call. Then report to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or 0300 123 2040 (in Scotland, Police Scotland on 101). Forward any scam texts to 7726, and report phishing emails to report@phishing.gov.uk.
faq: What is APP fraud or a push payment scam?

Authorised push payment (APP) fraud is when a scammer tricks you into sending money yourself, by bank transfer, rather than stealing it. They impersonate your bank, a seller, a tradesperson or the police and invent an urgent reason to pay — often telling you to move money to a 'safe account'. Because you authorised the payment, it can be harder to reverse. UK Finance recorded £576.4 million lost across 248,070 APP cases reported by its members in 2025 — a major high-loss category within payment fraud, measured on that dataset rather than across all UK crime.
Can I get my money back if I was scammed into a bank transfer?

Possibly. Mandatory protections apply to qualifying UK-to-UK Faster Payments and CHAPS APP claims by individuals, microenterprises and charities. Reimbursement is normally expected within five business days of a claim, but exclusions, a stop-clock of up to 35 business days, a possible excess of up to £100 (not for vulnerable consumers) and an £85,000 mandatory cap can apply. Report promptly and normally within 13 months of the last relevant payment.
What is the 159 number?

159 is a service backed by Stop Scams UK and participating banks and phone providers, much like 101 for the police. If you get a call, text or email about a payment and you're unsure, hang up and, if your bank supports it, call 159 to be connected safely to your bank before moving any money. If it does not connect, use the number on the back of your card or another official bank route you find independently. Your phone provider sets the price of a 159 call, so it is not necessarily free and may not be included in your allowance.
Someone overpaid me and wants a refund — is it a scam?

Treat it as likely fraud until your bank, payment provider or marketplace verifies the original payment and tells you how any reversal should be handled. The overpayment scam works by 'paying' you too much (often with a fake transfer, cheque or reversed payment) and asking you to refund the difference before the original payment is shown to have failed. Do not send a separate refund, and never return money to different details from the ones it arrived from. Check the transaction only in your provider's official app or service, and ask your bank, payment provider or the marketplace to verify it and, if it is not good, reverse the original payment through its own route. Do not release goods while the provider shows the payment as pending or disputed, and be wary of any buyer who overpays 'by mistake'.

government.title: Government Scams UK: HMRC, DVLA, DWP & More
government.description: Scammers impersonate HMRC, the DVLA, DWP, the Home Office and TV Licensing. Spot fake UK government texts, emails and letters, and check and report them safely.
government.intro:
Government impersonation scams use the names you can't ignore — HMRC, the DVLA, the DWP, the Home Office and TV Licensing — to make a fake message feel official. The lure is either a refund you're owed or a threat: a fine, arrest, a suspended benefit, or a visa or licence problem. Government departments do make genuine contact by text, email, phone and post, so the channel settles nothing — the safest move is always to verify an unexpected message independently through GOV.UK, your own account there, or a contact route you obtained from GOV.UK, never through the link or number in the message.

Not sure about a 'government' message? Paste it into our free AI scam checker for an automated second opinion. It is not a verdict and does not replace checking through an official route yourself.
sections: The most common UK government scams

HMRC is frequently impersonated — fake tax-refund texts and emails, plus threats of unpaid-tax 'arrest'. The DVLA is impersonated in fake car-tax renewal and refund emails. Benefit and immigration scams impersonate the DWP (Universal Credit) and the Home Office (UKVI visa messages).

Others include fake passport-renewal sites (HMPO), TV Licence demands, court-summons emails (HMCTS), and council-tax texts.
How government impersonation scams work

• The refund lure: 'You're owed a tax refund or car-tax refund — click to claim.' The link leads to a fake gov.uk-style page that harvests your card and personal details.
  • The threat lure: 'You owe tax, your benefit is suspended, there's a warrant for your arrest' — pressure designed to panic you into paying or sharing details.
  • The disguise: spoofed sender names ('HMRC', 'GOV.UK'), lookalike web addresses, and official-looking logos.
  • The payoff: stolen card and bank details, or harvested personal data — name, address, National Insurance number, even passport details from a fake 'identity check'.
How to check a 'government' message safely

• Go to gov.uk yourself. Search for the service (tax, vehicle tax, Universal Credit, passport) and sign in to your own account there — never via the link in the message.
  • Use HMRC's exact safety rule. HMRC's current guidance says it sends some genuine texts and some can include GOV.UK information or webchat links, but it will not ask for personal or financial information in a text. Compare the message with the current campaign list or check in your tax account.
  • Don't be rushed. A message demanding payment within hours or threatening immediate arrest is a serious warning sign; verify the claim directly with the department.
  • Ask the checker. Paste the message into our free AI scam checker for a second opinion.
What to do if you've responded or paid

• If you entered card or bank details, contact your bank immediately to block the card and report fraud.
  • Change the password for any account whose details you entered, and turn on two-step verification.
  • If you shared personal data (National Insurance number, passport details), watch for identity fraud and consider a credit-file check.
  • Keep the message as evidence, then report it (below).
How to report a government scam in the UK

Forward scam texts free to 7726. Report suspicious emails to the National Cyber Security Centre at report@phishing.gov.uk, and HMRC-branded scams specifically to phishing@hmrc.gov.uk. If you've lost money or shared details, report to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or 0300 123 2040 (in Scotland, Police Scotland on 101). You can also report fake gov.uk websites to the NCSC.
faq: Does HMRC text or email you about tax refunds?

HMRC does send some genuine texts and emails, including messages about Self Assessment repayments, and some genuine campaigns include GOV.UK information or webchat links. HMRC says it will not ask for personal or financial information in a text. Do not use an unexpected message to submit details or claim money; sign in through GOV.UK yourself and compare the message with HMRC's current campaign guidance.
How do I check if a DVLA or gov.uk message is real?

Don't use the link in the message. Go to GOV.UK directly, search for the service (for example vehicle tax), and use the contact or account route shown there. Treat any unexpected request to confirm payment details through a message link as suspicious, and watch for lookalike addresses with extra words or different endings.
I clicked a fake HMRC or DVLA link — what should I do?

If you only opened the page, entered no information, downloaded, opened or installed nothing and granted no access, close it, report and delete the message, and remain alert for a follow-up. If you opened a file or attachment, installed software or a profile, granted a permission, allowed remote access, saw a security warning, or the device has since behaved oddly, treat it as a possible device compromise: disconnect it where appropriate, install pending updates, run the security checks your device or security software provides, remove anything you did not deliberately install, and change your passwords from a device you trust. If you allowed remote access, end the session first, remove or disable the remote-access software, secure your accounts from another trusted device, check your email forwarding and recovery settings, and get trusted technical help if access may persist. If you entered card or bank details, contact your bank immediately to block the card and report fraud, and change any passwords you entered. If you shared personal data like your National Insurance number, watch for identity fraud. Report it to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.
Where do I report government scam texts and emails?

Forward scam texts free to 7726. Report scam emails to report@phishing.gov.uk (NCSC), and HMRC-branded ones to phishing@hmrc.gov.uk. If money or details were lost, report to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or 0300 123 2040 (Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland).

email.title: Phishing Emails UK: Spot a Fake, Check It, Report It
email.description: Fake bank, HMRC, PayPal, Netflix and Microsoft emails all run the same play. How to check a suspicious email safely and report phishing in the UK.
email.intro:
Email is where scammers do their most patient work. An email can carry a pixel-perfect copy of a company's branding, a hidden link, an attachment and a reply address that looks right at a glance. Your inbox is also the master key to everything else you own — password resets for your bank, your shopping accounts and your social media all land there — so an email scam that succeeds rarely stops at one payment.

Many phishing emails are one of two things: a manufactured problem ('your payment failed', 'your account is suspended') or a manufactured windfall ('you're owed a refund', 'exclusive presale tickets'). Both exist to make you act inside the message instead of checking the account itself. Not sure about one? Paste it into our free AI scam checker for an automated second opinion — it is a fallible assessment, not a verdict, so check the claim independently as well by opening the official app or typing the company's address yourself.
sections: The most common UK phishing emails

Bank emails are the classic: an 'unusual activity' or 'account locked' warning with a button leading to a convincing sign-in page — see fake HSBC 'verify your details' emails, Santander 'restore access' emails and NatWest 'unusual activity' emails.

Billing and subscription emails run the same play using services you really do pay for — a failed Netflix payment, a limited PayPal account, an Amazon order or refund problem, or a Microsoft account facing suspension.

Official-looking emails borrow a public body's authority: a tax rebate you can supposedly claim through a link, a DVLA vehicle tax or fine notice, a TV Licence payment failure, or a Companies House filing demand aimed at company directors.

Three more break the mould entirely: CEO fraud, where the sender appears to be your own boss; sextortion emails demanding cryptocurrency; and seasonal lures such as fake festival presale emails timed to a lineup announcement.
Which email have you actually got?

The right response depends on what the message wants you to do. Find your situation below.

  • A payment or account problem at a company you really use. Your instinct is to fix it immediately, and that instinct is the product being sold. Don't use the email — open the app or type the address yourself and see whether the same message is waiting in your account, as our Netflix billing and PayPal 'account limited' guides show.
  • A problem at a company you have no account with. Do not act through the message; report and delete it, while remaining alert to follow-up targeting.
  • A request to move money, change an invoice's bank details or buy gift cards, apparently from a colleague or supplier. That is business email compromise — read the CEO fraud guide before you touch the payment.
  • A threat to publish webcam footage unless you pay in cryptocurrency. These go out in bulk to addresses harvested from old breaches, and such a demand is usually part of a bulk bluff; the sextortion email guide explains how to respond without paying or replying. If real intimate images of you do exist, treat it as a different problem and use the response set out further down this page.
  • An offer you never asked for. Treat it as a likely phishing attempt; it may seek details, payment or malware installation — see the HMRC rebate email and festival presale patterns.
  • You downloaded a file, opened an attachment, installed an app, granted a permission, or your device has since behaved oddly. That is a possible device compromise rather than a simple phishing email, and it needs its own steps — see the device branch below.
  • Your own account sending mail you didn't write, or a login that no longer works. That is a compromise rather than phishing: work through how to recover a hijacked email account straight away.
How to check a suspicious email safely

• Never use the link, button or phone number in the email. Open the official app, or type the company's address into a new tab yourself, and look for the same problem inside the account.
  • Treat the sender address as a clue, not an answer. Display names are trivially faked and reply addresses can be spoofed. A lookalike domain — micros0ft.com for microsoft.com — is a strong warning sign, but a convincing address is not evidence a message is genuine.
  • Judge the request, not the channel. Banks, HMRC, TV Licensing and retailers all run genuine email campaigns, and some include links. No genuine bank employee will ask you to disclose or read out a full PIN, full password or one-time banking or security code. Enter a code only in the official app or site, for an action you initiated, understand and can match to the code message; never do it at an unexpected caller's direction — a criminal can talk you through a genuine app while dictating the action you are approving. For another support service, verify the request independently and follow the warning in the code message. Do not enter credentials into a page reached from an unexpected message.
  • Don't open unexpected attachments, and distrust any deadline measured in hours — it exists to stop you checking.
The expensive minority: invoice and CEO fraud

Email is a rare starting point for authorised push payment fraud but a disproportionately costly one. UK Finance's Annual Fraud Report 2026 attributes around 1% of APP fraud cases to email and about 7% of the money lost — figures, periods and sources are in our UK scam statistics dataset. The emails that get through tend to be the ones aimed at businesses and at people in the middle of a large payment.

That is the shape of CEO fraud and its invoice-fraud cousin: no malware and no fake login page, just a confidential, urgent request to pay a real-looking invoice into a new account. A genuine-looking internal address is not evidence the request is real — verify with the named person through a channel you already had, never the contact details in the email. A Companies House email demanding payment or your company authentication code deserves the same treatment: Companies House says it will not ask for a company authentication code by telephone or email, so start fresh at GOV.UK.
If you clicked, paid or replied

• Entered card or bank details? Contact your bank using the number on your card or statement or its official app. If your bank and phone provider participate, you can also dial 159; if it does not connect, use the number on your card. Your provider sets the price of the call. Ask for the card to be blocked.
  • Disclosed a password, or typed one into a page you reached from the message? Change it through the service's official app or an address you type yourself, then change it anywhere else you reused it, and turn on two-step verification or a passkey. Then check for forwarding rules, filters and recovery addresses you did not set — attackers add them to keep reading your mail after the password changes, which is why the account takeover checklist puts that step first.
  • Downloaded a file, opened an attachment, installed an app or granted a permission? Opening a link is not always the end of it. If you downloaded or ran anything, allowed a browser or device permission, saw a security warning, or your device has since behaved unusually — unfamiliar apps or profiles, settings you did not change, sudden battery or data use — install the pending operating-system and app updates, run the security checks your device or security software provides, remove anything you did not deliberately install, revoke permissions you did not intend to grant, and change your passwords from a device you trust. If the odd behaviour continues, get help from a trusted support route such as the device manufacturer's own support channel.
  • Sent money by bank transfer? Tell your bank immediately. Eligible domestic consumer payments by Faster Payments or CHAPS made on or after 7 October 2024 may fall within the mandatory APP reimbursement rules, subject to exclusions, an £85,000 cap, a 13-month outer reporting limit and a possible excess of up to £100 that cannot be applied to a consumer the firm assesses as vulnerable. Reimbursement is not guaranteed, and reporting quickly matters.
  • Shared personal details? Watch for identity fraud, check your credit reports, and consider a Cifas Protective Registration at cifas.org.uk.
  • Being threatened with real intimate images? Do not pay and do not reply. Keep the evidence — the message, the account name and any payment demand — and report an immediate threat to the police. Adults in the UK can get support from the Revenge Porn Helpline. StopNCII may help if you are currently 18 or over, were 18 or over when the image or video was created, are the person depicted, and still have the file; it creates a hash on your own device for use by participating platforms and does not upload the image. The sextortion email guide sets out the steps in order.
  • Keep the email as evidence, then work through the remaining payment, account and identity steps in our scam recovery checklist.
How to report a scam email in the UK

Forward suspicious emails to the National Cyber Security Centre at report@phishing.gov.uk. HMRC-branded phishing goes to phishing@hmrc.gov.uk and Companies House-branded phishing to phishing@companieshouse.gov.uk. Most large brands also run their own abuse mailbox or an in-product 'report phishing' option; take the current address from the security or help pages of their official website rather than from the email in front of you. If you have lost money or shared details, report it to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland. A suspicious website or link can be reported to the NCSC through its own suspicious-website reporting form, and a suspicious SMS text can be forwarded free to 7726.
faq: How can I tell a phishing email from a real one?

Judge what the message asks you to do, not how it looks. Branding is easy to copy and genuine organisations do send emails containing links. No genuine bank employee will ask you to disclose or read out a full PIN, full password or one-time banking or security code. Enter a code only in the official app or site, for an action you initiated, understand and can match to the code message; never do it at an unexpected caller's direction — a criminal can talk you through a genuine app while dictating the action you are approving. For another support service, verify the request independently and follow the warning in the code message. Do not enter credentials into a page reached from an unexpected message.
Does the sender's email address show whether a message is genuine?

No. Display names are easy to fake and reply addresses can be spoofed, so a convincing sender is not evidence the email is real. A lookalike domain — extra words, hyphens or a swapped character such as micros0ft.com — is a strong warning sign, but its absence tells you nothing either way. Check the claim inside your own account instead.
I clicked a link in a phishing email — what should I do?

If you only opened the page and entered nothing, that does not automatically mean the device is compromised: close it, report the suspicious website to the NCSC, run the security check your device or security software provides, and check for any unexpected download, app, profile, permission or security warning. If any occurred, or the device behaves unusually, follow the device-compromise steps below. If you entered card or bank details, contact your bank using the number on your card or statement or its official app. If your bank and phone provider participate, you can also dial 159; if it does not connect, use the number on your card. Your provider sets the price of the call. If you disclosed a password or typed one into that page, change it through the service's official app or an address you type yourself, then anywhere else you reused it, turn on two-step verification, and check your email for forwarding rules or filters you did not create. If you downloaded a file, opened an attachment, installed an app, granted a permission, saw a security warning or your device has since behaved oddly, treat it as a possible device compromise: update the device, run its security checks, remove anything you did not install, and seek trusted support if it continues.
Should I reply to a sextortion email or pay?

No. These are sent in bulk and the demand is usually part of a bulk bluff, often quoting a password taken from an old data breach to make it feel specific. Paying invites more demands and replying confirms your address is live. Change that password if you still use it and report the email. If real intimate images of you do exist, keep the evidence, still do not pay, report an immediate threat to the police, and get support from the Revenge Porn Helpline. StopNCII may help if you are currently 18 or over, were 18 or over when the image or video was created, are the person depicted, and still have the file.
Where do I report a scam email in the UK?

Forward it to the National Cyber Security Centre at report@phishing.gov.uk. Use phishing@hmrc.gov.uk for HMRC-branded messages and phishing@companieshouse.gov.uk for Companies House-branded ones. If money or personal details were lost, report it to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.

travel.title: Travel Scams UK: Fake Holidays, Flights & Bookings
travel.description: Fake package holidays, flights, villas and transfers, plus timeshare and compensation cons. How to check ATOL, ABTA and a booking before you pay.
travel.intro:
Travel fraud has a cruel shape. The sums are large, they are often paid by bank transfer weeks or months ahead, and the loss surfaces at the worst possible moment — at the check-in desk, or on a doorstep in another country. Holiday, flight and accommodation payments usually fall inside the purchase scam category of authorised push payment fraud, and purchase scams accounted for 71% of all APP fraud cases reported by UK Finance in its Annual Fraud Report 2026, with £118.1 million lost. That £118.1 million is the total for all purchase scams in UK Finance member data — every kind of goods-and-services-that-never-arrived fraud — and is not a travel-loss figure; the numbers and their sources are in our UK scam statistics dataset.

Many travel scams are one of three things: a trip that was never booked, a message about a booking you really do hold, or a contract you were pressured into signing. Work out which one you are looking at and the right checks follow. Unsure about an offer or a message? Paste it into our free AI scam checker for an automated second opinion — it is a fallible assessment, so verify the seller, the protection and the booking independently before you pay.
sections: Which travel scam are you looking at?

• A seller is offering you a trip. This is the fake-supply group, where the holiday, flight or property may not exist. Start with the package holiday scam guide or, if it is the seller you cannot place, how to verify a travel agent. Flight-only deals are covered in the fake airline ticket guide, independent rentals in holiday let scams, and sailings in cruise scams.
  • You already have a booking and have been messaged about payment. That is impersonation of a real transaction — see Booking.com payment messages, or the TUI and Jet2 guides if the approach came through social media or WhatsApp.
  • You are being asked to sign or pay at a presentation. These are long-term contracts rather than one-off thefts: read holiday club scams and timeshare scams first.
  • Someone has contacted you about money you are owed from a past trip. Cold callers offering to recover flight or holiday compensation are covered in the fake claims handler guide.
  • You are paying for help with a visa. No adviser can guarantee an outcome — see UK visa application scams.
  • You have just landed and need a car. Arrivals halls have their own version, from bogus transfer sites to touts. Use an official licensed taxi rank, or a transfer you pre-booked through a route you verified yourself, and never accept an unlicensed tout. In Great Britain a private-hire vehicle or minicab must be pre-booked rather than hailed: in England and Wales the booking must be through a licensed private-hire operator, while Scotland runs its own vehicle, driver and booking-office regime, where a booking may be made with a licensed owner-driver or through a booking office. Northern Ireland instead licenses taxis in classes A to D, and some classes may be hailed or taken from a rank in defined circumstances, so do not carry the Great Britain pre-booking rule across. Wherever you land, an approach offering an unbooked ride is a warning in itself.
What ATOL and ABTA actually tell you

These two names do most of the reassurance work in travel advertising, which is why they get borrowed.

  • ATOL is the CAA scheme connected to flight-inclusive travel. A qualifying flight-inclusive package sold by or through an ATOL holder should come with an ATOL Certificate as soon as you pay anything, including a deposit, and that certificate names the ATOL holder providing the protection. Some flight-only bookings made through an ATOL holder are protected too, while cruise-only bookings generally are not.
  • A travel agent does not need its own ATOL. It can sell a protected trip on another company's licence, so check the holder named on the certificate using the CAA's Check an ATOL service rather than only searching the shop front.
  • A missing certificate is a serious warning sign, not a verdict. Ask who the ATOL holder is, confirm it with that holder using contact details you found independently, and ask the CAA for advice if the answer does not stack up.
  • ABTA is not ATOL. Check any ABTA claim on ABTA's own member search: a logo on a website is a picture, not a membership, and a false claim to either scheme is itself reportable, as the fake travel agent guide explains.
Warning signs — and two tests that do not settle it

Across fake packages, flights, villas and agents the same signs recur: a price far below every other source for the same dates; payment pushed towards a bank transfer, especially into a personal account whose name does not match the business; a deal that exists only inside a social ad, a WhatsApp thread or a DM; a seller who will not produce an invoice, terms or verifiable supplier details; and pressure to pay before you can check anything. Event accommodation is a seasonal example: a listing selling Glastonbury accommodation before the Festival's own booking information is published is harder to corroborate, so check the address itself, the platform's own record of the listing and host, and the current information published by the Festival before any money moves.

Two checks that settle less than people think. A booking confirmation or itinerary can be fabricated, so the document is not evidence in itself. More importantly, failing to find your booking in an airline's manage-my-booking page is not evidence that no ticket exists — agent, group, charter and partner bookings are not always visible there. Contact the airline directly, ask whether a valid reservation and e-ticket exist in your name, and preserve the answer; the fake airline ticket guide walks through that conversation. Cheap checks worth doing: reverse image search the photographs and confirm the address exists, which can expose copied photographs or an implausible address in a fake independent holiday let before money moves.
Messages about a booking you really do hold

The hardest travel scams to spot arrive with your real reference number, the correct dates and the right property attached. A fraudulent message can appear inside a genuine thread when an account used to send it has been compromised, and other data exposures are possible, so appearing in the right thread is not authentication. Booking.com payment messages are the best-documented example: Booking.com says it will not ask travellers for card details by email, phone, text or WhatsApp, and warns against a bank-transfer request that differs from the payment-policy details in the booking.

TUI and Jet2 impersonations come from the other direction — an implausible flash sale or a prize for a competition you never entered, pushing you towards a payment outside the company's own checkout. Either way the check is identical: leave the message where it is, open the app or type the company's address yourself, use Manage My Booking, and compare what is being demanded with the payment policy in your original confirmation.
Contracts, memberships and 'money you're owed'

Holiday clubs and timeshares are sold as long-term contracts rather than one-off purchases, and the documented risks sit in the paperwork: commitments that can run for years, ongoing management, membership or maintenance charges that can change, restrictive cancellation and resale terms, and high-pressure selling at a long presentation. Same-day pressure is a serious warning; a legitimate trader should let you read the terms and obtain independent advice. Take the full contract away, work out what it would commit you to and cost each year, and get independent advice before signing anything. A qualifying timeshare or long-term holiday product carries a 14-day withdrawal right under the 2010 Regulations, but that right attaches to those defined product types rather than to every holiday-club arrangement, so check whether it applies to the specific contract instead of assuming it is your exit.

Holders of those contracts — and travellers generally — are then targeted a second time. Fake claims handlers cold-call about flight or holiday compensation you never claimed, and it works because the underlying compensation rules are real. Claim flight-delay compensation directly from the airline for free. If you consider paying a representative, verify the firm and the specific service through the regulator that actually covers it; do not treat an FCA Register entry as approval of an aviation claims service. Paying for help with a UK visa application calls for the same caution. Start at GOV.UK. A paid immigration adviser should be registered with the Immigration Advice Authority, authorised through an approved professional body, or otherwise lawfully exempt. Verify which route applies before paying or sharing documents.
How to pay safely, and what to do if you have already paid

• Pay by card through the company's own checkout. Refuse a request to transfer money to a personal account that does not independently match the business. A bank transfer does not provide card chargeback or Section 75 protection, although an eligible domestic consumer transfer may fall within the mandatory APP reimbursement rules.
  • Know what card payment gives you. Where a credit agreement funded the trip, Section 75 may apply: it needs the required credit-to-supplier relationship and a cash price of more than £100 and no more than £30,000, counted per item or qualifying set, so paying on credit does not guarantee cover. Chargeback is separate — a card-scheme process with scheme-set deadlines rather than a statutory right.
  • If you paid by transfer, tell your bank as soon as you can. Eligible domestic consumer payments by Faster Payments or CHAPS made on or after 7 October 2024 may fall within the mandatory APP reimbursement rules, subject to their exclusions, an £85,000 cap, a 13-month outer reporting limit and a possible excess of up to £100 that cannot be applied to a consumer the firm assesses as vulnerable. Reimbursement is not automatic, and speed matters.
  • Treat a follow-up fee as unverified until you check it. Do not pay an unexpected follow-up “release”, “tax”, “admin” or “upgrade” fee until you have verified it with the airline, hotel, tour operator or platform through a channel you opened yourself. Repeated fees to unlock a booking or refund are a strong scam warning.
  • Save the evidence before the listing disappears: advert, messages, confirmation, any ATOL certificate and the payment record. Then work through the account and identity steps in our scam recovery checklist.

Reporting. Tell the platform that carried the advert, and the airline, hotel or tour operator named on the confirmation so it can investigate misuse of its brand. Report a false or unverifiable ATOL claim to the CAA, and a false ABTA claim to ABTA. If you have lost money, report it to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland. Scam emails go to report@phishing.gov.uk, and a suspicious SMS text can be forwarded free to 7726.
faq: Does an ATOL Certificate mean my holiday is protected?

It is strong evidence, but read it rather than glance at it. A qualifying flight-inclusive package sold by or through an ATOL holder should generate a certificate as soon as you pay anything, including a deposit, and it names the ATOL holder providing the protection. Check that named holder on the CAA's Check an ATOL service, and make sure the trip, passengers and holder match what you booked.
The travel agent has no ATOL of its own — is that a scam?

Not by itself. An agent can sell a protected trip on another company's ATOL and does not need one, so the question is who the ATOL holder is. Ask, check that holder independently, and confirm the relationship using contact details you found yourself. A seller who will not name the holder is the real warning sign.
My booking doesn't show in the airline's manage-my-booking — has the agent stolen my money?

Not necessarily. Agent, group, charter and partner bookings are not always visible in an airline's online lookup, so a failed search is not evidence that no ticket exists. Contact the airline directly, ask whether a valid reservation and e-ticket exist in your name, and keep the response. If it confirms there is nothing, contact your bank promptly and report it.
A message about my hotel booking asked for card details — is it genuine?

Check it independently before doing anything, even if it quotes your real reference inside an existing thread: a fraudulent message can appear in a genuine thread if the account used to send it has been compromised, so the thread is not authentication. Booking.com says it will not ask travellers for card details by email, phone, text or WhatsApp. Open the app or type the site's address yourself and compare the request with the payment policy in your confirmation.
I paid a travel company by bank transfer and the holiday doesn't exist — can I get my money back?

Possibly, and speed matters. Tell your bank immediately and report it as fraud. Eligible domestic consumer payments by Faster Payments or CHAPS made on or after 7 October 2024 may fall within the mandatory APP reimbursement rules, subject to exclusions, an £85,000 cap, a 13-month outer reporting limit and a possible excess of up to £100 that cannot be applied to a consumer the firm assesses as vulnerable. Keep the advert, confirmation and payment record, and report it to Report Fraud in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.

marketplace.title: Marketplace Scams UK: Facebook, eBay, Vinted & More
marketplace.description: Buying or selling on Facebook Marketplace, eBay, Vinted, Gumtree or Depop? Spot fake sellers, fake buyers and off-platform payment cons, and report them.
marketplace.intro:
A recurring marketplace scam pattern is an attempt to move a transaction away from whatever protected checkout or messaging flow the platform offers. On classified local sales, where cash on collection may be normal, the equivalent warning is pressure to pay a deposit or follow an unexpected payment or courier link before inspection. The move can be into a bank transfer, a WhatsApp thread, a 'friends and family' payment, or a link sent in chat. Where a platform runs its own checkout, that checkout is where buyer and seller protection lives, so a push to leave it is a strong warning where the platform offers an eligible protected checkout.

The scale is not marginal. Purchase scams — paying for goods that never arrive — made up 71% of all authorised push payment fraud cases in UK Finance's Annual Fraud Report 2026, and online shopping was the most commonly reported scam type among victims in Citizens Advice's 2025 Scams Awareness survey, at 26%. Both figures, with publishers and periods, are in our UK scam statistics dataset. Unsure about a listing, a buyer or a 'payment confirmation'? Paste it into our free AI scam checker for an automated second opinion — it is a fallible assessment, so still check the account, the item and the payment state in the official app yourself.
sections: Buying or selling? Find your situation

Marketplace fraud attacks buyers and sellers in completely different ways, so start with which side of the deal you are on.

  • Buying, and the seller wants a deposit or transfer before you have seen the item. This is the classic fake-seller pattern on local and classified listings: Facebook Marketplace, Gumtree, Preloved and Shpock all see the same 'transfer to hold it' script, whatever protected checkout the platform may also offer.
  • Buying on a platform with its own checkout, and the seller offers a discount to pay outside it. That is protection-stripping — see eBay scams, Vinted warning signs, Depop off-app payment cons and Etsy sellers who ask you to pay off-site.
  • Selling, and the buyer has produced a payment confirmation, an overpayment or a link to 'release' funds. Read Facebook Marketplace fake buyers and Vinted buyer scams before you post anything.
  • You have had an email from the platform itself about a fee, a held payment or a listing about to be removed. That is platform-impersonation phishing, such as the fake eBay listing fee notice.
  • It is a car. Vehicles can involve especially large deposits or payments — see Autotrader car scams.
  • It is somewhere to live or stay. Property listings attract deposit fraud: Rightmove rental scams and fake or hijacked Airbnb listings.
What platform protection actually covers

Marketplaces are not interchangeable, and the difference decides what happens when a deal goes wrong. Protection is conditional and transaction-specific everywhere: eligibility, evidence requirements and deadlines vary by platform and by deal.

  • Platforms with their own checkout — eBay, Vinted, Etsy, Depop, Airbnb — publish protection terms that apply to eligible purchases paid for through the platform itself. Pay outside it and you may fall outside the platform's protection altogether, which is exactly why an off-platform 'fee-free' discount is such a strong warning sign. Our Etsy guide and Vinted guide set out how each platform's cover works, and the eBay guide explains why keeping messages as well as payment on the platform matters if you later need to evidence a dispute.
  • Local classified listings — Facebook Marketplace's local ads, for example — introduce a buyer to a seller rather than processing the payment, so an ordinary local cash-on-collection deal should not be assumed to carry buyer protection at all.
  • Gumtree now sits in between. Gumtree now offers Buy Now, secure payment and Buyer Protection through Mangopay for eligible delivery-enabled items up to £250; the button appears only on eligible ads. Ordinary local and in-person listings should still not be assumed to carry that protection. Check the exact ad and complete any protected checkout inside Gumtree. Our Gumtree guide covers the deposit-before-viewing script that still dominates local deals.
  • Preloved is different again. Preloved says it does not itself handle ordinary transaction payments, although some listings may offer an optional Trustap transaction. Verify that option from the listing or account you opened yourself and read the current Trustap terms; never trust a buyer-supplied “Preloved payment” link. Our Preloved guide covers the rest of the classified-deal checks.
  • Shpock needs its own line. Shpock's current help says its Buy Now feature and Wallet have been discontinued. For a new deal, do not assume that Shpock supplies an in-app payment or Buyer Protection step. Users may agree collection or arrange tracked delivery themselves, but Shpock says it has no courier service of its own. A supposed “Shpock courier”, or an unexpected courier or payment link, is a strong warning sign; our Shpock guide covers the deposit-before-collection script.
  • The payment type matters as much as the platform. A PayPal 'friends and family' payment is not a purchase payment and does not attract purchase protection. Refuse a request to transfer money to a personal account that does not independently match the business or seller you verified. A bank transfer does not provide card chargeback, Section 75 or marketplace buyer protection, although an eligible domestic consumer transfer may fall within the mandatory APP reimbursement rules. Report a transfer you have come to doubt to your bank quickly.
Selling: a payment confirmation is not a payment

Every seller-side con attacks the same gap — between seeing evidence of a payment and having the money. A screenshot, an email that appears to come from a payment provider, or a 'funds held pending dispatch' notice can all be fabricated. Verify the status in your own bank or platform account, opened independently, and never from an email or a screenshot someone has sent you. Do not dispatch while the platform still shows the payment as pending. Facebook Marketplace fake buyers and the overpayment refund request are common variants, and the overpayment version needs particular care: a credit you can see in an account can still be held, recalled, reversed or investigated, so do not send a separate 'refund' without first contacting your bank or the platform through a channel you opened yourself and confirming the position.

Watch too for the variant aimed at the seller: a link to 'confirm your card' or 'verify your account' to release funds. As the Vinted buyer scam guide explains, a genuine sale is settled through the platform's own order and payment process, so check the order and payment state in the official app rather than acting on a link sent in chat, and treat any request to enter card details to 'release' money you are owed as a scam. Collection deals have their own version: a message from a courier you did not arrange, whatever brand it claims, is a warning sign rather than a delivery arrangement.
Collection day, cars and viewings

Some marketplace losses happen face to face, or should have. Never pay for a car you have not seen and inspected, and be sceptical of any seller who cannot meet, wants a deposit to hold the vehicle, or claims the marketplace itself will hold your money in escrow — that last line recurs in these cons, so check any such scheme with the site itself before relying on it. For a long-term residential rental, view the property and verify the landlord or agent before sending a holding deposit or rent. For a short-stay platform such as Airbnb, prepayment may be normal, so keep the reservation and payment entirely inside the official platform. A landlord who is conveniently abroad and will post the keys after a transfer is the classic rental scam, and a fake or hijacked Airbnb listing works by moving you off the platform.

For an in-person handover, meet somewhere public and busy in daylight, take someone with you, inspect the item, and hand nothing over until the money has arrived — the advice in our Gumtree guide and Preloved guide applies to any classified deal. A live video call can help corroborate that the seller has the item in front of them, but it is not proof of ownership, identity or a safe transaction. Seasonal listings deserve extra care: bargain festival tents and camping gear on Vinted appear every summer from sellers who want to move the conversation to WhatsApp.
If you have already paid, or handed over the item

• Contact your bank or card issuer first, on the number on your card or statement, and report it as fraud. If you paid by card, ask about chargeback — a card-scheme process with scheme-set deadlines rather than a statutory right.
  • Where a credit agreement funded the purchase, Section 75 may apply, subject to the required credit-to-supplier relationship and a cash price of more than £100 and no more than £30,000, counted per item or qualifying set. Marketplace purchases often involve intermediaries, so paying on credit does not guarantee cover.
  • If you sent a bank transfer, eligible domestic consumer payments by Faster Payments or CHAPS made on or after 7 October 2024 may fall within the mandatory APP reimbursement rules, subject to exclusions, an £85,000 cap, a 13-month outer reporting limit and a possible excess of up to £100 that cannot be applied to a consumer the firm assesses as vulnerable. Reimbursement is not guaranteed — report quickly.
  • Report inside the platform too, while the account still exists: the listing, profile and message thread are the evidence it needs. Then screenshot everything and work through the payment, account and identity steps in our scam recovery checklist.
How to report a marketplace scam in the UK

Use the platform's own reporting tools first — on the listing, the profile and the message thread — because that is what lets the platform investigate while the evidence still exists. It may restrict or remove the account as a result, but no report can guarantee that outcome, so protect your own position as well. Platform-branded phishing emails should be reported through the platform's current security or help route, which the platform publishes on its own site rather than in the email itself, and forwarded to the National Cyber Security Centre at report@phishing.gov.uk. If you have lost money or shared bank details, report it to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland. A suspicious SMS text can be forwarded free to 7726. For consumer-rights help, use the service for your nation: Citizens Advice in England and Wales on 0808 223 1133, Advice Direct Scotland in Scotland on 0808 800 9060, or Consumerline in Northern Ireland on 0300 123 6262.
faq: Is it safe to pay a Facebook Marketplace or Gumtree seller by bank transfer?

Treat a request to transfer money for an item you have not seen as a strong scam warning sign on a classified site. A bank transfer has no card chargeback and no marketplace buyer-protection process, though an eligible domestic consumer transfer may still fall within the mandatory APP reimbursement rules, subject to exclusions and limits. An ordinary local listing should not be assumed to carry buyer protection. View and collect in person, pay on collection, and walk away from any seller who insists on a deposit to 'hold' the item.
A buyer sent me a payment confirmation — can I post the item?

No. Screenshots and confirmation emails can be fabricated, and a 'funds held pending dispatch' notice is a known con. Check the payment status in your own bank or platform account, opened independently, rather than from anything the buyer sends, and do not dispatch while the platform shows the payment as pending. If the buyer says they have overpaid and wants the difference back, remember that a credit you can see can still be held, recalled, reversed or investigated: do not send a separate refund without first contacting your bank or the platform through a channel you opened yourself.
A seller offered a discount if I pay outside the app — what is the risk?

You may fall outside the platform's protection, which applies only to eligible purchases paid through its own checkout, and eligibility, evidence requirements and deadlines vary. Paying outside the app may remove platform protection regardless of why the discount is offered. Decline and keep an eligible transaction inside the platform; if the seller refuses, walk away. Keeping the conversation on the platform matters too, because the thread is the evidence if you later need to raise a dispute.
I have been scammed on a marketplace — can I get my money back?

It depends on how you paid. Contact your bank or card issuer immediately: card payments may allow a chargeback under card-scheme rules, and where a credit agreement funded the purchase Section 75 may apply if the required relationship exists and the cash price was more than £100 and no more than £30,000. For an eligible domestic consumer bank transfer by Faster Payments or CHAPS on or after 7 October 2024, the mandatory APP reimbursement rules may apply, subject to exclusions, an £85,000 cap and a 13-month outer reporting limit.
Where do I report a fake listing, buyer or seller?

Report it inside the platform first, using the report options on the listing, profile and messages: that lets the platform investigate and it may restrict or remove the account, though no report guarantees it. Report platform-branded phishing emails through the platform's current security or help route, and forward them to report@phishing.gov.uk. Report any financial loss to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.

phone.title: Phone Scams UK: Spot a Fake Caller and Check Safely
phone.description: Vishing calls, fake bank fraud teams and spoofed caller ID: the UK phone scam patterns, how to verify a caller safely, and how to report a scam call.
phone.intro:
Phone scams — vishing, or voice phishing — put a convincing person or recording on the line and give you a reason to act before you think. The caller may claim to be your bank's fraud team, a broadband provider, HMRC, the police, or a salesperson with an offer that expires today. What they want is nearly always one of four things: a payment, a one-time passcode, your security details, or remote access to a device.

Genuine banks, telecoms firms and government departments do telephone people, so the channel settles nothing — the request is the discriminator. End the call on anything pushing you towards those four things, then ring back on a number you found yourself. Unsure about a call or voicemail? Describe it to our free AI scam checker for an automated second opinion. It is a fallible assessment, not a verdict, so still verify the caller independently.
sections: The main UK phone scam patterns

Fake bank fraud teams are a persistent pattern: your account is 'under attack', and the fix is often moving money or reading back a code. See fake HSBC fraud team calls and Santander impersonation calls — and the same script often arrives dressed as law enforcement in a police impersonation call.

Telecoms calls claim a fault, a virus or a refund and end with a request for remote access: see fake BT technical support calls, TalkTalk support call scams and Virgin Media 'virus on your connection' calls.

Official-sounding calls lean on a name you cannot ignore — a fake HMRC tax call threatening arrest, an automated 'your National Insurance number is suspended' robocall, or a DVLA call about failed vehicle tax. Retail impersonation works identically in an automated Amazon order call.

Cold-call sales approaches apply commercial rather than fearful pressure: free solar panels under a 'government grant', or an offer to unlock your pension early that our pension liberation guide shows can trigger a substantial HMRC charge on top of the loss.

Suspicious calls to mobiles appear to be becoming less common, while telecommunications-originated APP fraud remains disproportionately costly. Ofcom's February 2026 survey found 32% of mobile users had received a suspicious call on their mobile in the previous three months, down from 40% in 2022. Separately, UK Finance's Annual Fraud Report 2026 attributed 17% of APP cases and 28% of APP losses to telecommunications. APP here means authorised push payment — a transfer the victim was deceived into making. The two measures count different things: one is calls received by mobile users, the other is the contact channel recorded against APP cases and losses. Both are dated in our UK scam statistics research.
Caller ID is not evidence of identity

Start from this: the number on your screen is not evidence of who is calling. Caller ID can be spoofed, including in some cases a genuine bank number — our number spoofing guide explains how it is done. Ofcom's Do Not Originate list helps providers identify and block calls from numbers an organisation does not use for outbound calls, which narrows the problem — but Ofcom notes that adding a number to the list is not a guarantee that all such calls will be blocked, and its advice remains to hang up and call the organisation back on a number from its official website. The reverse holds too: an unfamiliar number is not by itself a scam. Judge the call on what it asks you to do.

Do not press a number on an unexpected recorded call. A keypress can connect or advance the call; hang up and verify the claim independently.
Work out what kind of call you are dealing with

Run an unexpected call through these questions in order. The first 'yes' tells you which situation you are in.

  • Asked to move, send or withdraw money? Treat it as an attempted authorised push payment scam; there is no such thing as a 'safe account'. The courier version asks you to hand cards, cash or valuables to someone at your door. City of London Police recorded more than £21 million lost to courier fraud specifically across 1,891 reports in 2025 in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, which excludes Scotland, with victims aged 76 to 96 accounting for around 62% of those reports. It is a figure for that one pattern and that one reporting area, not for phone fraud as a whole. See the police impersonation guide.
  • Asked to read out a one-time passcode, PIN, password or full card number? A code can authorise a payment, a login, a password reset, a device registration or a change to your account, so reading one aloud can complete an action you never intended. No genuine bank employee will ask you to disclose or read out a full PIN, full password or one-time banking or security code. Enter a code only in the official app or site, for an action you initiated, understand and can match to the code message; never do it at an unexpected caller's direction — a criminal can talk you through a genuine app while dictating the action you are approving. For another support service, verify the request independently and follow the warning in the code message.
  • Asked to install software or share your screen? That is the remote-access pattern: the tools are genuine, the request is what fails. See what remote access can expose.
  • Asked to confirm personal details 'for security'? They may be assembling an identity-fraud profile rather than chasing an immediate payment.
  • A recording with a threat and a keypress? A bulk campaign. Hang up without pressing anything.
  • A sales pitch that expires today? The urgency is the product. Take the details, end the call, and research the company yourself.
How to check a caller safely

• End the call, then verify independently. Hang up. Use a different phone where possible. If you must use the same landline, allow time for it to clear and first call someone you know on a number already saved. Then call the organisation on a number from its official site, statement or card. Ofcom's current scam-calls page says to hang up, take your time and call the organisation back using a number from its official website; it sets no fixed number of minutes to wait, so treat any specific delay you have read elsewhere as practice rather than regulator guidance.
  • Dial 159 yourself after an unexpected call claiming to involve your bank or bank account. It is the route you reach by dialling 159 that cannot be spoofed, and 159 never calls you. Stop Scams UK says the service covers firms representing more than 99% of UK retail current accounts, which is not a guarantee for every handset or network. Your own provider sets the price of the call and it may not be included in your allowance, so check that if cost matters — and if it does not connect, use the number on your card.
  • Use a number you already hold — the back of your card, a paper bill, or an address you typed in yourself. Never one the caller gave you, and never one from a pop-up or a search advert.
  • Check the claim, not the caller. Sign in to your own account or app and see whether the problem actually exists.
  • Ask the checker. Paste what the caller said into our free AI scam checker for a second opinion once you have verified independently.
If you have already paid or shared details

• Contact your bank immediately on the number on your card, or by dialling 159. Act straight away rather than waiting to see what happens.
  • If you were talked into authorising a bank transfer yourself, ask about mandatory APP reimbursement. It covers eligible domestic consumer Faster Payments and CHAPS payments made from 7 October 2024, with an £85,000 cap, a possible excess of up to £100 that cannot be applied to a consumer the firm assesses as vulnerable, a 13-month claim limit and a set of exclusions — a route worth pursuing, not a guaranteed refund.
  • If you granted remote access, disconnect the device, remove the software, and change key passwords from a different trusted device — our remote access scam guide sets out the full clean-up.
  • If you shared personal details, watch for identity fraud and consider a Cifas Protective Registration at cifas.org.uk after checking the current fee.
  • Work through our scam recovery checklist, and be wary of any follow-up offer to 'get your money back' — recovery fraud targets people who have just been defrauded.
How to report a scam call in the UK

Report to your bank first if money or account details are involved — dial 159 or use the number on your card. Then report it to Report Fraud (formerly Action Fraud) at reportfraud.police.uk or 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland. Dial 999 if someone is on their way to your door to collect cards, cash or valuables. Tell the impersonated company too, through its official website or the number on your bill. If the same campaign reached you by text, a suspicious SMS text can be forwarded to 7726 free of charge. Reporting a suspicious call is a separate step: from a mobile, forward the caller's phone number to 7726, which Ofcom says is free of charge. For consumer-rights help, use the service for your nation: Citizens Advice in England and Wales on 0808 223 1133, Advice Direct Scotland in Scotland on 0808 800 9060, or Consumerline in Northern Ireland on 0300 123 6262.
faq: Can a scam caller really display my bank's real number?

Caller ID can be spoofed, including in some cases a genuine bank number, so treat the display as unreliable and judge the call on what it asks you to do. Ofcom's Do Not Originate list helps providers block calls from numbers an organisation never uses for outbound calls, but Ofcom notes that adding a number to the list is not a guarantee every such call is blocked. If money is involved, hang up and dial 159 yourself, or use the number on the back of your card.
What is 159 and when should I use it?

159 connects you to your bank when you dial it yourself, much as 101 works for the police, and it is that outbound route that cannot be spoofed — 159 never calls you. Stop Scams UK says participating firms represent more than 99% of UK retail current accounts, which is not a guarantee for every network or handset. Your provider sets the price of the call and it may not be included in your allowance; if it does not connect, use the number on your card.
How do I tell a genuine bank fraud call from a scam?

Banks do telephone customers about suspicious activity, so the call itself is not the signal — the requests are. A genuine bank will not ask you to move money to another account, read out a one-time passcode, disclose a full password or PIN, or install remote-access software. If any of those come up, end the call and ring back on the number from your card or by dialling 159.
I gave a caller my details or a security code — what should I do?

Contact your bank immediately on the number on your card or by dialling 159 and ask them to secure the account. Change passwords for any account you discussed, starting with email, and turn on two-step verification. If you installed anything at the caller's request, disconnect the device and remove the software. Then report it to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.
